practice.solution: we → **they**, visited → **had visited**, last Sunday → **the previous Sunday**. 'Last Sunday' keeps the anchor of the speaking day; 'they visited' skips the rung; 'the next Sunday' points the wrong way in time.
practice.shortcut: last → the previous; next → the following. Never mix the two.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Ravi said to me, "Meet me here tomorrow morning."
options: Ravi asked me to meet him there the next morning.
Ravi asked me to meet him here the next morning.
Ravi asked me to meet me there the next morning.
Ravi told me that meet him there the next morning.
practice.solution: An instruction reports with to + V1: **asked me to meet him there the next morning.** me → him (the speaker becomes third person from outside), here → **there** (the reporter stands elsewhere), tomorrow → the next. 'Here' keeps the speaker's position; 'meet me' leaves the quote's pronoun; a that-clause cannot carry an order.
practice.shortcut: Orders: asked/told + object + to + V1; here → there.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Grandmother said, "This mango tree was planted by my grandfather."
options: Grandmother said that that mango tree had been planted by her grandfather.
Grandmother said that this mango tree had been planted by her grandfather.
Grandmother said that that mango tree was planted by her grandfather.
Grandmother said that that mango tree had been planted by his grandfather.
practice.solution: The connector that is followed by the demonstrative that — **said that that mango tree** is correct, not a typo. this → that, my → her, and was planted steps to **had been planted**. 'This mango tree' keeps the pointing word; 'was planted' skips the rung; 'his grandfather' gets the speaker's gender wrong.
practice.shortcut: that that is legal: conjunction + demonstrative.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

My aunt said to me, "Do you like filter coffee?"
options: My aunt asked me that did I like filter coffee.
My aunt asked me if I liked filter coffee.
My aunt asked me if did I like filter coffee.
My aunt asked me if I do like filter coffee.
practice.solution: Yes/No question → **asked me if I liked filter coffee**: the do disappears and its tense lands on liked; you → I (the listener is the reporter). 'That did I' uses a statement connector and keeps the do; 'if did I' keeps the inversion; 'if I do like' keeps the do and the present.
practice.shortcut: do/does/did die; the tense moves to the main verb.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The stranger asked the shopkeeper, "Is there a pharmacy near here?"
options: The stranger asked the shopkeeper if there is a pharmacy near there.
The stranger asked the shopkeeper that there was a pharmacy near there.
The stranger asked the shopkeeper if there was a pharmacy near there.
The stranger asked the shopkeeper whether was there a pharmacy near there.
practice.solution: **asked the shopkeeper if there was a pharmacy near there** — is steps to was and here to there. 'Is a pharmacy' skips the rung; a that-clause cannot report a closed question; 'whether was there' inverts the order after the connector.
practice.shortcut: Yes/no → if/whether + statement order; here → there.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The interviewer asked me, "Why do you want this job?"
options: The interviewer asked me why I wanted that job.
The interviewer asked me why did I want that job.
The interviewer asked me that why I wanted that job.
The interviewer asked me why I want that job.
practice.solution: **asked me why I wanted that job** — the wh-word leads, the order is statement order, do dies (want → wanted), you → I, this → that. 'Why did I want' keeps the auxiliary and the inversion; 'that why' stacks connectors; 'why I want' leaves the present behind.
practice.shortcut: wh + subject + verb. do/does/did never survive.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said to him, "Where have you kept the spare key?"
options: She asked him where had he kept the spare key.
She asked him that where he had kept the spare key.
She asked him where he has kept the spare key.
She asked him where he had kept the spare key.
practice.solution: **asked him where he had kept the spare key** — have steps to had, you → he, and the order flattens to statement order. 'Where had he kept' inverts the auxiliary; 'that where' stacks connectors; 'has kept' stays on the direct rung.
practice.shortcut: have/has → had inside a past frame; order flattens.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The teacher said to the boys, "Do not make a noise in the library."
options: The teacher ordered the boys not to make a noise in the library.
The teacher ordered the boys do not make a noise in the library.
The teacher ordered the boys to make a noise in the library.
The teacher ordered the boys not making a noise in the library.
practice.solution: Negative order → **ordered the boys not to make a noise in the library** — not sits before to, and the imperative verb keeps its base form. 'Do not make' leaves the quote inside the frame; dropping not reverses the command; 'not making' swaps the infinitive for a gerund.
practice.shortcut: Negative orders: not + to + V1. The not travels with the frame.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The officer said to the clerk, "File these papers immediately."
options: The officer ordered the clerk to file those papers immediately.
The officer ordered the clerk to file these papers immediately.
The officer ordered the clerk filing those papers immediately.
The officer ordered to the clerk to file those papers immediately.
practice.solution: **ordered the clerk to file those papers immediately** — the order takes to + V1 and these shifts to those. 'To file these papers' leaves the demonstrative unshifted; 'ordered the clerk filing' breaks the infinitive; 'ordered to the clerk' inserts a to that ordered never takes.
practice.shortcut: Order = to + V1; this/these → that/those.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The patient said to the doctor, "Please prescribe a milder tablet."
options: The patient requested the doctor prescribing a milder tablet.
The patient requested the doctor to prescribe a milder tablet.
The patient requested to the doctor to prescribe a milder tablet.
The patient ordered the doctor to prescribe a milder tablet.
practice.solution: Please → **requested the doctor to prescribe a milder tablet.** The listener follows requested directly; the verb after to stays bare. 'Requested the doctor prescribing' swaps the frame; 'requested to the doctor' inserts an impossible to; 'ordered the doctor' has a patient commanding a doctor — the tone is absurd.
practice.shortcut: please → requested + object + to + V1. Never 'to the doctor'.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The elder said to the boy, "Always speak the truth."
options: The elder advised the boy speaking the truth always.
The elder advised that the boy speaks the truth.
The elder advised to the boy to always speak the truth.
The elder advised the boy to always speak the truth.
practice.solution: General moral instruction is advice: **advised the boy to always speak the truth.** 'Advised the boy speaking' drops the to-frame; a that-clause with speaks reports a statement, not advice; 'advised to the boy' is a to that advised never takes.
practice.shortcut: Advice → advised + object + to + V1; always/never before the verb.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The players said, "Hurrah! We have clinched the series."
options: The players exclaimed with sorrow that they had clinched the series.
The players exclaimed with joy that they have clinched the series.
The players exclaimed with joy that they had clinched the series.
The players told with joy that they had clinched the series.
practice.solution: Hurrah is joy: **exclaimed with joy that they had clinched the series** — have clinched steps to had clinched and we → they. 'With sorrow' reverses the emotion; 'they have clinched' skips the rung; 'told with joy' is not the exclamation frame.
practice.shortcut: Hurrah → joy; Alas → sorrow. Then run the ordinary checks.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The farmer said, "Alas! The locusts have eaten the entire crop."
options: The farmer exclaimed with joy that the locusts had eaten the entire crop.
The farmer exclaimed with sorrow that the locusts had eaten the entire crop.
The farmer exclaimed with sorrow that the locusts have eaten the entire crop.
The farmer exclaimed with sorrow that the locusts ate the entire crop.
practice.solution: Alas is grief: **exclaimed with sorrow that the locusts had eaten the entire crop** — have eaten steps to had eaten. 'With joy' celebrates a disaster; 'have eaten' stays on the direct rung; 'ate' under-shifts the present perfect.
practice.shortcut: Alas → with sorrow; have + V3 → had + V3.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The manager said to the clerk, "You were absent yesterday."
options: The manager told the clerk that he was absent the previous day.
The manager told the clerk that he had been absent the previous day.
The manager told the clerk that he had been absent yesterday.
The manager said to the clerk that he had been absent the previous day.
practice.solution: Four checks, all needed: said to → **told**; were steps to **had been**; yesterday → **the previous day**; you → **he**. 'He was absent' skips the rung; 'yesterday' keeps the dead anchor; 'said to the clerk' refuses the verb change. Each decoy drops exactly one check.
practice.shortcut: Verb, time word, pronoun, frame — tick all four before answering.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The girl said to her mother, "I cannot find my ribbon anywhere."
options: The girl told her mother that she can not find her ribbon anywhere.
The girl told her mother that she could not find my ribbon anywhere.
The girl said to her mother that she could not find her ribbon anywhere.
The girl told her mother that she could not find her ribbon anywhere.
practice.solution: said to → **told**; can steps to **could**; I and my follow the speaker → **she/her**. 'Can not find' splits and refuses the shift; 'my ribbon' hands the ribbon to the reporter; keeping 'said to her mother' leaves the direct frame standing.
practice.shortcut: can → could; both I and my belong to the speaker.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

The teacher told the students that the earth revolves around the sun.
options: The teacher said to the students that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said to the students, "The earth revolved around the sun."
The teacher asked the students, "Does the earth revolve around the sun?"
The teacher said to the students, "The earth revolves around the sun."
practice.solution: Reverse conversion: told returns to **said to**, the connector that dissolves, and the quotes return with the full stop inside. The universal truth keeps its present — no un-shifting needed. Leaving 'that' inside the quote is the classic reverse fault; 'revolved' un-shifts a truth that never shifted; the question version invents a different sentence.
practice.shortcut: Reverse = frame back, connector out, quotes in. Truths stay put.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

The doctor advised him not to eat fried food.
options: The doctor said to him, "Do not to eat fried food."
The doctor advised him, "Not to eat fried food."
The doctor said to him, "Do not eat fried food."
The doctor said to him, "You are not eating fried food."
practice.solution: The advice frame advised + not to + V1 reverses to the negative imperative: **said to him, 'Do not eat fried food.'** — the not goes back inside the quote as do not. 'Do not to eat' carries the frame's not into the quote wrongly; 'advised him, ...' keeps the reported verb with direct words; the eating version changes the sentence.
practice.shortcut: not to + V1 → 'Do not + V1' in the quote.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The clerk said to the manager, "Shall I close the register now?"
options: The clerk asked the manager that if he should close the register then.
The clerk asked the manager if he should close the register then.
The clerk asked the manager if he should closed the register then.
The clerk asked the manager if he will close the register then.
practice.solution: Shall I...? (seeking the listener's instruction) reports as **asked ... if he should close the register then** — shall steps to should and now to then. 'That if' stacks connectors; 'should closed' corrupts the verb after should; 'if he will close' skips the modal shift entirely.
practice.shortcut: Shall I...? → asked if + should/might; now → then.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The boy said to the shopkeeper, "Could you tell me the price of this toy?"
options: The boy asked the shopkeeper that could he tell him the price of that toy.
The boy asked the shopkeeper if he could tell him the price of that toy.
The boy asked the shopkeeper if he can tell him the price of that toy.
The boy asked the shopkeeper if he could tell me the price of that toy.
practice.solution: **asked the shopkeeper if he could tell him the price of that toy** — the polite could stays (already one step down), you → he, me → him, this → that. 'That could he' stacks a connector and inverts the order; 'can tell' would be wrong even in the direct quote's shape here; 'tell me' leaves the quote's pronoun.
practice.shortcut: Polite could stays could; swap you/me by the SONA anchors.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The guest asked the host, "What is being served for dinner?"
options: The guest asked the host what was being served for dinner.
The guest asked the host what is being served for dinner.
The guest asked the host what was being served for dinner?
The guest asked the host that what was being served for dinner.
practice.solution: **asked the host what was being served for dinner.** — is steps to was and the question mark becomes a full stop. 'What is being served' leaves the present inside a past frame; the question-mark version is wrong on punctuation alone; 'that what' stacks connectors before a wh-word.
practice.shortcut: Reported questions end in a full stop. Check the last character.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The child asked her mother, "When will the rains come?"
options: The child asked her mother when would the rains come.
The child asked her mother when the rains will come.
The child asked her mother when the rains would come?
The child asked her mother when the rains would come.
practice.solution: **asked her mother when the rains would come.** — will steps to would and moves AFTER the subject (statement order); the question mark dies. 'When would the rains come' is question order inside a reported clause; 'will come' skips the shift; the final ? is wrong punctuation.
practice.shortcut: After the wh-word: subject, then verb. Full stop at the end.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The coach said, "The trials may be postponed till next week."
options: The coach said that the trials might be postponed till the following week.
The coach said that the trials may be postponed till the following week.
The coach said that the trials might be postponed till next week.
The coach said that the trials must be postponed till the following week.
practice.solution: Two shifts in one line: may steps to **might** and next week becomes **the following week**. 'May be postponed' shifts the time but not the modal; 'till next week' shifts the modal but not the time; 'must be postponed' swaps the modal for its stronger cousin.
practice.shortcut: Modal AND time word must both move. Half-shift = wrong.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "I could have finished the work yesterday."
options: He said that he could have finished the work yesterday.
He said that he can have finished the work the previous day.
He said that he could have finished the work the previous day.
He said that he could have finish the work the previous day.
practice.solution: could have is a frozen unreal form — it stays as it is; only yesterday moves to **the previous day** and I to he. 'Yesterday' left behind is the half-shift; 'can have finished' un-freezes the modal the wrong way; 'could have finish' drops the participle.
practice.shortcut: could have / would have / might have never shift. Move the time words.
